note: Reader-facing release notes for returning readers (modules/reading-switches.mjs). Newest first. Plain words, no internals.

notes: Your way through, a trial at your desk (Scriptorium, or ?try=way-through): set a chapter aside, or keep two people out of the same room, and the book goes round them. The chapter after one you stepped over says what it held, a passage told another way is marked, and a button puts the words back. It is written as one line of Spw you can read, change by hand, or pass to someone for a visit. If you never turn it on, the book is exactly as it was.

Chapters can say why they are here, a trial in the switches (or ?try=reasons): each chapter ends with a closed fold saying why the book has it, and a line one edit away from something it says. Guess now, check against a later chapter, or keep it open.

Exactly One Pie: the people have themes (Setup, Characters). Mr. BoonWAP, Mr. BaneWAP and BoneWAP are one tune turned three ways. The Genie is a stack of fifths that comes home a little sharp. The porter knocks in three meters. A mime is a bar of rest. The melody takes the instrument of whoever is carrying, a chapter leaning toward low magic sings in open fourths (by your lens, or your carries there), and a spill closes on the openings of everyone you met, in order. If you have played before you keep the short calls until you choose.
The margins remember two more things. A pane struck in the lanes is counted in Chapter Six's lantern glass, and a beaver's pace is counted beside the dam in Chapter Eight.
In the deck, each person now says what they want and what they cannot do, what they remember of you, and, folded, why they are drawn that way.
The part of the book that reads Spw is about a quarter of its old size to download, so bracework and the game's rules are ready sooner on a slow connection.

Exactly One Pie keeps better time. A chapter slower than the one before it used to leave the lanes empty and the beat silent for a while, longest in chapters Four, Seven, Ten and Thirteen. The lanes now go on from the same place in the bar. The rhythms you have found sit exactly on the beat, and six chapters lean a little, each for a reason in its story: the grove in Two answers late, and the clowns in Six and Nine shuffle.

A room says its chord once as it opens, strummed far off, and the chord changes on the beat. A chapter carried to its end closes with a few notes that tell how it went: home, when it is carried; home and brighter, when it is won back from the mimes; left hanging, when they take it. Then the next chapter's tune begins.

A pie tilting too far can be heard: a low note on the side it leans to, drifting out of tune, and back in tune as it settles. What is sung has a soft echo in the chapter's time. A run of good things fills the room's chord in, a fifth, then its third, then the room's colour, and what comes down the lanes is heard once as it nears, in the stuff it is made of.
If Music is set to only what happens (Setup, Music and rhythm), the lanes stay as sparse as they were: no room chords and no tilt note.

A hop hangs at the top. A clear there steadies the pie and brings the next slice on, and a hop pressed while you are still in the air leaves the ground again as soon as you land. A throw dead centre counts for more than a throw that is only close, and a throw from the hang, from a held poise, or off a wall counts for more again.

Exactly One Pie unlocks a few things as you read and play, each one sentence long, each with a page of its own at lore.land/pie/unlocks/: two registers at once, the rhythm groove, and a new one, In the pocket, where moving on the beat of a rhythm you have found counts toward low magic. Rooms read, wonders kept, rhythms found and carries finished all count toward them, reading most. Any of them can be tried for a visit from its page, and nothing you already had is taken away.

Ask the land for a charm at lore.land/charm/: a wonder to meet, a rhythm for the lanes, a recipe beside the story, a line kept for someone without their name. It opens autonomous.feedback, the post the Scriptorium reads, and asks for no name or email. The old form there never reached anyone; if you wrote one, the scribes would be glad of it again.

The Scriptorium is about your desk and how the book is made. Who supports the book is one short line now: nothing here is paid for, and if anything ever is, it will wear a mark beside the story, never in it.

Exactly One Pie keeps time now. Each chapter has its own tempo, key and tune: what comes down the lanes arrives on the beat, and the things you catch spell out the chapter's tune, which you hear once, softly, as the chapter begins. Boof has three notes of his own when he crosses.

Every chapter hides a rhythm in one of its rooms. When the lanes say something here keeps time, listen: step, hop or throw along with it and it is yours, and from then on it plays under your carries in its own voice. There are fifteen to find.
⚙ Setup has a new section, Music and rhythm: hear only what happens, the rhythms you have found, or those and the room's chord held underneath; and let the screen glow on the beat or on each bar.
Opened as an app on a phone, the front page fits the screen again: the row that puts the game and the atlas a tap away had made it wider than the phone, which zoomed out to show it all.
On a slow connection a page is always this release's own: a copy kept from an earlier visit is shown only when the network is gone.

Pages hold still while they load. Chapters, the desk, the almanac, the folios and the game used to jump a little as their pieces arrived; now each keeps the room it will need, so the line you started reading stays where it is.

Every page has the same menu now, and Play is in it. Each page also opens on one thing worth a look: what is new if you have been here before, a way in if you have not — today's wonder to look for, the newest chapter to carry the pie through, a saying for the fold.

If you have been here before, a small card in the corner says what changed since your last visit — every release you missed, not just the last two — and any page it names is a link. Every chapter, in order lists the whole book again, Book Two included.

Keeping the book for reading offline now keeps everything each page needs to work, and it lasts past the next release. The game and spwashi's hand can be kept too. Text no longer waits on a font from elsewhere, and the game's rule reader loads when you start to play.

On a sheet of ruled boxes, spwashi lettered the alphabet by hand; it is traced here into two typefaces, a solid one and one that keeps the pen line as drawn. At lore.land/?/texture.website/@spwashi you can write any word in that hand, letter by letter in boxes like the sheet's, and see the sounds the word is made of underneath.

The address is part of the play. Every part of it reads: ?/ asks, texture.website is where it belongs, @spwashi whose hand, !Boof the words written, =~2 how it is tuned. Write or tune and the address changes with you, so what you made can be passed along — and read before it is opened.

Words can be made on something: paper, a wash, a drip, hatching, honey, glass or a storm, each with its own ground, its own way of setting the hand, and its own physics — the letters become things you can pick up and throw, and they come back as the material says. Add &factshift.center/?ground to the address and the same physics is said in factshift.center's terms, ready to open there.

A ? in the address passes it through spw.quest: ?clarify reads it to you, ?align tidies it, ?mutate varies it, ?edit makes changes written into it, ?enhance fills in what is missing, ?resonate finds what echoes it on the folios. Each one leaves a receipt saying what it did.

Where the sheet had no letter (numbers, marks, the Spw sigils), a pen measured from the hand draws one, in a dashed box that says it was penned. A line of Spw tunes how the hand is shown — wandering, leaning, bouncing, as scanned, or with its measure showing — and the page always says what was changed on purpose.

spwashi's hand comes with a curriculum: ten plans, each something to make and a question to ask about how pictures and words are made, written for readers of different ages to do together. It also reads spwashi's folios for textures, figures and sayings, each linked to the piece it came from on spwashi.com.

Every artifact now has a picture: a drawn study of the thing itself in one light, at the head of its card in your almanac and on the card that opens when you find it in a chapter. Ones you have not found yet show only as a shape in the dark, enough to know them when the prose turns them up. They are studies, the way Fourteen and Fifteen's plates began; the painted plates come later.

Exactly One Pie paces itself better. A new card no longer stops you in the middle of dodging: it waits for a breath (a quiet stretch of road, or a turn between rooms) and says it is waiting. Captions no longer talk over each other; they take turns, and the ones that matter most go first. If you have carried the pie before, cards still open at once as they always have; ⚙ Setup › Cards and captions lets anyone choose.

⚙ Setup is sorted into five sections (screen and pace, buttons and arrows, taps and swipes, the story, cards and captions), each saying what it is set to before you open it, and the game's buttons are drawn icons now, the same on every phone and computer.

Your almanac has two new shelves. Antiques are the old things the land keeps, the forgiving kiln, the storm weight, the press stones and others, each with who made it, who keeps it, and what it remembers (they were contrivances before; anything you kept is still kept). Artifacts are what a scene leaves behind: the horn button, the slice in waxed paper, the gate-book entry, the signed DAMAGE slip, the relit torch, the crier's note, two receipts on the bridge rail. Two artifacts are made in the lanes rather than found in the chapters: a plate from the stack, and a found line.

Every creature in the bestiary now says how it moves and who misreads it, and things you have not found yet let slip a clue: how a creature moves, who keeps an antique, what left an artifact. In Exactly One Pie the land's own behave by their kind: fliers ride at hat height and are kept only from a hop, burrowers only from the ground, roamers wander across the lanes, antiques wait longest, artifacts lie on the road close by; each wears its kind's own frame, as on its new badge in the almanac and in the chapters.

The book and Exactly One Pie now wind through each other. A rumour you come across in a chapter's margins is said in the lanes when your carry reaches that chapter: clowns going home from the plaza's edge in Six, a placard with nothing on it in Eleven, prints in the frost on the Thursday in Fourteen, plates stacked by the spring water in Thirteen, and a new one on the hill in Four about baneberries.

What you do in the lanes is told back in those margins, marked 'since the lanes': how many clowns went home from the plaza, how many foretellings were stepped on before they could be said, how many boonberries you ate in passing, how many times something warm was passed close, how many plates are waiting by the water, how many placards the mimes have put up. Reading gives the carry something to look for, and carrying gives the margins something new to say.

The book and Exactly One Pie now look at each other from the side rather than retelling each other. In the margins of Chapter Six, clowns go home delighted from somewhere off to the side of the plot; in Eleven, someone has pasted a placard with nothing on it to the garden wall; in Thirteen, plates are stacked by the cold spring water, taller than the meal could have been.

In the lanes, Chapter Fourteen is the Thursday nobody kept: nobody comes down the lanes at all until the last of it, when Friday arrives with everyone in it. When the pie spills, the card counts the plates the carry left for the washer-up, beyond the frame. Every card now names the trope its thing belongs to, and what the book shows of it that the lanes cannot.

Exactly One Pie can arrange its panels for the screen you are on (⚙ Setup › Panels: Arranged for this screen; already on if you have not carried the pie yet). On a phone held up, every panel stays in view at once: the caption rides the top of the lanes, two lines of the book sit under them, and the heights fold small; on a phone on its side or a tablet the panels stand in a column beside the lanes; on a wide screen the book is on one side and the panels on the other. The lanes never shrink below half the window to make room; a panel gets smaller first. As a room opens, the caption and the story come forward; when danger is close, whatever lies over the lanes thins so you can see through it. Nothing changes size while you play.

⚙ Setup has more ways to move: arrows on the screen in a row, on either side, or as a cross; under the screen, at its edges, or over it. On a phone, choosing these shows the arrows instead of the pad. You can choose what a tap in the lanes does (throw there, walk there, step toward it, hop, or nothing), what a double tap does, and whether a quick swipe up hops while a slower drag still steps ahead.

With the story on the road, its words can be kept: walk over a glowing word to read it, land a hop on any word to mark it, or let a slice come down on one to feed it (that slice is not wasted). Every five words kept make a found line, said in the caption and shown again when the pie spills. In ? Ask, tap a word to see the sentence it came from.

Exactly One Pie has more music in it. Each room of the story colours the chapter's key by its sign, and what the lanes give sings that room's chord: catches, bank shots and deft landings carry on one melody between them, and answers land on the chapter's own pulse. Keep a run of good things going and the land joins in, the room's chord rising softly under you until a knock breaks it; and when the pie spills, as it must, the tune comes home.

The lanes have depth now: there is a room around them, open air in the field and walls close by in the city, and things far up the lanes sound farther off than things at your feet. The instruments have their own voices: a celesta for catches, a marimba for deft landings, a vibraphone for boonberries, two kalimbas for a share, and a music box for wonders.

Exactly One Pie sounds kinder on the hundredth go. No sound plays quite the same way twice; one heard over and over (footsteps, mostly) grows quieter and softer the longer it keeps up, and is itself again after a breath. Catches, bank shots and deft landings walk the chapter's key as they come, so a run of them is a little tune rather than one blip again; a hop is a plucked string that climbs as hops chain; the clowns' honks are kazoos in the chapter's key, a step higher for each WAP in a combo; and knocks are duller thuds than they were, still out of key.

In Exactly One Pie the story's rooms shape the lanes: while a room passes, things of its own kind come up more often (a room of strikes brings more to strike, a room of ground its stones and holes, a room of meetings people to share with), and as the passage nears the next room the lanes begin to lean its way.

Every room has a verb, from the sign it is written under: struck, answered, taken, seen, joined, kept, lifted, marked, let go, tuned, measured, made. Do a room's verb while it passes and the room is cast; the chapter page then says so beside the room. A room's banner in the lanes says its sign at first, then what that sign makes of the lanes, then how to cast it, as you come to know it.

Whatever goes well or badly in the lanes is now told as something asked and measured, with the way it leans the chapter and the room it happened in: the inspected carry shows where in the story each of your moments happened, with a way back into that room.

The scriptorium has a new room, the projection: the book's Spw laid on a disk that is larger inside than it looks, where whatever you stand on sits at the centre, what it touches rings it, and the short loops through it can be walked round, each thing showing first its spell, then what it means once stood on, then what it is for once a loop is walked; every chapter's inventory now ends with a door to it.

Throw and hop can be arranged in ⚙ Setup: in the middle of the step buttons as before, on either side of them, or as an A/B pair on a diagonal, hop low and throw high, like a pair of buttons under a right thumb. Either can be swapped, Hands mirrors them, and the buttons come small, medium or large. On a phone the same choices arrange them around the pad.

Sizing the cabinet by its corner now snaps: it holds at the sizes the window offers (fit the window, medium, as wide as there is room) and steps between them so every lane is a whole number of pixels wide, saying the size beside the corner as you drag.

The story can be read in the lanes now. The carry goes through a chapter much faster than anyone reads, so the lanes tell it at reading speed: as a caption at the top of the screen that stays up as long as its words take to read, or painted on the road a phrase at a time. On a phone, where the story beside the game is out of sight while you play, it starts as a caption.
On the road, a wonder's own words glow: step onto one as it passes underfoot and you have read it, which feeds the crust a little and leans the chapter toward the fairy tale.

⚙ Setup has layouts that set several things at once (Lanes first, Reader, Tactician, Comic page), a table of what each view makes easier or harder (across, ahead, height, timing, the story), and the cabinet can be sized by dragging its corner ◢; the story strip under the screen by dragging its foot.
In Exactly One Pie, ⚙ Setup opens over the screen instead of pushing it down, and a tap outside it or Escape puts it away without pausing the game.

A tidying pass behind the scenes: the game's styles were folded together where they had been layered over one another, its own colours (the mimes' violet, a knock's red, the silent-film card's gold) now have names, and nothing you see changed except where it was meant to.

Exactly One Pie fits the window now: it measures what play needs in view and gives the screen the rest of the window's height. On a wide screen the caption and the heights strip move beside the cabinet so the lanes can be as large as the window allows; on a phone they follow the controls, below.
The controls are a single row of icons (each still says its name to a screen reader and on hover), or icons and words if you prefer, above the screen or below it, as you choose in ⚙ Setup.

The story beside the game moves a passage at a time by default, each paragraph holding still at the line while it passes, which is easier to read; the line can sit high, middle or low, and the old smooth motion is still there. The caption box can be hidden, and pressing Play brings the whole cabinet into view.

Installed on a phone or a computer, Lore.Land now leads with the game and the atlas: Play and Atlas are the first shortcuts on its icon, its front page offers both at the top, and keeping the book offline keeps them too.
In Exactly One Pie the controls are at the top of the cabinet now, with a ❚❚ Pause button for screens that have no Esc key.

⚙ Setup gathers what you can change about the cabinet: how big it is, the pace of the whole world (gentle, as written, or brisk), whether the story runs beside the screen or in a strip under it, how big the story's words are, and whether the heights strip shows. Every choice is kept.
Pinch works on the game page too: over the story it sizes the words, on the cabinet's frame it sizes the cabinet. The lanes and the pad are left to your fingers for playing.
Pinching to size the words in a chapter works again on iPhone and iPad, where Safari had been zooming the whole page instead.
The scrolling story beside the game is easier to read: the passages not going by stay legible, and its words grow with your setting.

When the pie spills, the card is a prompt now: what happened in a line, then what to try next, drawn from what actually happened (it was low enough to hop, the mimes took a chapter, there are rooms still unread), with a button or a link to do it, and Play again.

Beside the screen, The carry, inspected lays out everything the carry did as tiles, marking your bests. Tap one for what it is, what each is worth, how this carry compares with your best and with every carry so far, the stills of those moments if the show kept them, and the same thing as a line of Spw; the whole carry is there as a spell too.
Copy as a prompt writes the carry as a scene, in the book's voice, to write or draw from or pass along.

Hopping in Exactly One Pie is easier to read: under the screen, ⤒ Heights turns the lane you stand in on its side, so you can see how high each thing stands (in the air, tall, low, underfoot) and what a hop does about it. The arc of a hop taken now is drawn over it, whatever it would clear is ticked, and a line says what is next: hop in 0.3 s, hop now, step aside, or only a high hop. Three pips show the chain toward a high hop. Both ways of seeing height are options: the ⤒ marks worn in the lanes, and the side view, whose parts (the arc, the words, the bands, the chain) each turn on or off, looking one, two or nearly three seconds ahead.
A hop that clears something at the top of its arc is in time, and a run of them is a rhythm: it leans the chapter toward low magic, and somebody notices.

The game reads like a comic page now: the lanes, the lane from the side and the show are inked panels; on a big moment their frames flash together; and a small meanwhile panel cuts away to someone elsewhere, in a mood, with a word. Boof hums along to a rhythm, Mr. BaneWAP thinks of a scheme, a clown says WAP.

Reading and playing now feed each other both ways. Rooms you have read steady the pie in their chapter, and a chapter read room by room makes the pies tell you what they know of it. What they let slip in the lanes appears beside the room it is about, in their voice, and what you have not heard yet leaves a quiet note of how to hear it. Every chapter now has something of theirs to find.

The almanac writes where you are as a spell, every collection at once (rooms read, wonders kept, cards turned, palettes begun, lore heard, people met), and names the next chapter with rooms still unread.
Fixed: a rare moment, just after a card was put away, when time in the lanes could run backwards for a frame and stop the game.

In Exactly One Pie the mechanics are drawn where they act: every gift in force is a badge over the hat with what is left of it, a leaning pie shows a CATCH chevron on the side to step to, a combo is a row of pips with the time left to keep it going, and stillness fills a ring under the carrier's feet until it turns gold.

Whoever is under the hat now shows how the carry is going: a small smile, a level look as the needle turns, a grin after a WAP, a worried brow (and a bead of sweat) as the pie tilts, an ouch at a knock.

Each carrier has a knack of their own: the figure's finer aim, the porter's long hold on an arrow, the clerk's quick feet between hops, the Genie's true aim after a satisfied clown, and the clown's bigger feelings. Their cards show the knack and four bars of how they carry.

Every character now has a model sheet on the game's design table: five moods, the traits a reader could name, a temperament in a line, their knack if the hat settles on them, and their colours. Meeting someone for the first time, their portrait looks surprised.

In Exactly One Pie, every point says where it came from: a small chip rises from the spot in the lanes, in the colour of the way it leans the chapter (fairy tale, absurd reality, low magic) or for the pie against the mimes. Beside the screen the points are said in words as they come, and How points work lays out every weight from the rules in play, marked where you have tuned one. The card at the spill says how the whole carry was scored.

A new ▢ Show button (or V) gives the game a window under the screen: the last thing that happened, as a still, with what it was worth. Press it again for the board, the lanes as a plain board where every thing is a token for what it does, with a mark where a hop clears it; the lanes as drawn shrink into the window. The last few stills are kept beside the screen.
A card turned in the lanes now rises in its own light, says what it can be worth before you play it, reads its spell aloud, and keeps Play on in reach at its foot; the notes for testers fold away.

Spells are easier to read everywhere: a long one is laid out a line a part, each sigil sits on a small coloured key, a row of dots at its head shows its shape at a glance, and a hairline along its top carries its colours in order, so spells of one shape look related.

The land can answer in a register now: cast one as a spell (on the game's tuning desk, by link with ?bias=pov, or with the new trial switch) and the pops, notices and receipts now and then come back as POV, plot twist or core memory: unlocked, while the story keeps every word of its own. One register is always free; layering several is a trial for now.

The seed atlas belongs to the book again: every study wears its sigil and a seal of what it is made of, and waits veiled in its chapter's colours until you open that chapter. Like every room, wonder, palette, card and person in the almanac, the cast and the game, it can show you what in the book is like it, by what things are made of and never by who else has looked.

At the end of every chapter a folded page now says what it is made of in one spell, and keeps every sigil it holds: what you have found is lit and takes you back to it, and what you have not yet found only tells you where to look.

Everyone in the book now has a portrait, in one style, wherever they turn up: on the cast on the front page, on their card in the almanac, in the notice when you first meet them in a chapter, and at the end of the chapter where you did. Someone you have not met yet is a silhouette with a question mark, and the cast says where their name first comes up.

The portraits travel: on the game's design table each one copies or downloads as a standalone picture, with who they are as a Spw spell, and the whole set copies as one file for prints, other pages or a design tool.

In Exactly One Pie the lanes now have height, and say so: every hazard's ring marks whether a hop clears it (⤒), only a high hop does (⤒⤒), or it is too tall (▮). Hops hang at the top, squash and stretch, and chain: hop again soon after clearing something and the next goes higher, and the third clears the posts.

From Chapter Four arrows on the track set your aim and hold it (every throw on an arrow is Perfect), and weathercocks by the lanes swing it. From Six a brass horn starts a game, Vane Alley or The Parade; from Ten, The Long View, where the road recedes to a far point and you see what is coming sooner.

? Ask slows the lanes and lets you tap anything to learn what it is in the story and which passage of the book was going by; ◇ Labels keeps every thing's name on. Tapping a sigil in any spell now primes it and a second tap casts it, the way spells are cast on spwashi.com. And the buttons say Play.

Every spell can be played now: press ▶ and it sounds its shape, each sigil a voice (a question rises, a measure ticks, a body holds a low note under everything inside it), each part lighting as it sounds. A spell made of glass or frost or flour sounds and looks like it.

In Exactly One Pie the numbers in a spell are dials: scroll over one, or drag it, and the lanes retune at once. The tuning desk under the game holds every dial, including how far a swipe goes and how much staying ahead is worth. Copy any spell and paste it anywhere on the page and the lanes read it; every card is read aloud as it turns; impacts pop and splat a good deal more.
In the Scriptorium, the loom of stories: everyone the book is for, written as a spell, laid side by side so you can see, and hear, what they share.

Every section of every chapter is a room now, with a name, a kind and a line of its own air: a window you may only look in, a room to stand in, a gathering where everything arrives together, a passage you go through. Each is written as a small Spw signature at its door, and a strip at the head of the chapter lights the rooms you have read. Try reading one room at a time with ?try=room-by-room.

In Exactly One Pie every card shows the spell it runs on, lit: each sigil in its own colour, each bracket knowing its pair, and what each part does said as you touch it. The game reads its rules from one Spw file now, and the chapters lean toward fairy tale, absurd reality or low magic by what you actually did, which each chapter page will tell you.
The game is also a test of the language it is written in: on its page, the rules can be compared, round-tripped and roughed up on purpose, and what turns up is written down for the workbench.

Exactly One Pie on a phone: under the screen now sits a pad that is the lanes in small. Touch or slide to where you want to stand and the carrier walks there, and each column warms red as something comes down that lane. Hop and throw sit under your other thumb; slide along throw to turn the needle. A switch swaps them for the other hand.
The page under the game is in three parts now, Playing, Keeping and Making, with an index that stays in reach, and every label on it reads in every cover.

The berries foretell. A boonberry shows you the way something will go well, a moment before it does; whether it showed you or you remembered it, nobody can say. A baneberry says what will go wrong, and it goes wrong because it was said. A boneberry promises nothing and feeds you, savoury, and it tastes of wherever it grows. The chapters tell all three, and Boof keeps a map of what keeps what: it is on the front page now.

In Exactly One Pie the needle stays where you leave it; turn it with Q and E, point, or drag it round from the pie. Every power-up does in the lanes what it does in the book, keeps you company while it lasts, and is a short Spw spell you can change on the page and pass along. Each carry writes itself back as a card of where it went and why. Drags step as you go, the sound sits in each chapter's key, and zen gives the screen the room the words leave.

The edge of every page is the edge of the land now: a root line with the torch-ants' lit street along it, and one light over the paper instead of a wash. Every cover was checked for contrast and the dark ones read properly.

Every chapter has its own palette now, colours and lettering mixed from one of the laminated folios. Finish a chapter and you keep a layer of it: read to its end for the colour, carry the pie through it for the type, keep its wonders for the light. The chapter wears what you keep; a switch at its end sets it aside.
Everyone in the book has a card, turned the first time their name comes into view in a chapter or the first time you meet them in Exactly One Pie. Both keep the same deck.

The almanac has two new shelves, Palettes and Cards. A kept palette can be carried away as a Spw atom or as CSS tokens, and the contents on the front page show the palettes you have begun along the foot of each plate.

Exactly One Pie has cards now: the first time you meet a character, an obstacle or a power-up, its card turns, telling who or what it is in the story, what it does in the lanes, and where the book first has it. Choose From the beginning, with introductions to meet everyone in order from Chapter One.
Under the screen: fold the story beside it away, switch on Zen for a carry with nothing popping up, or go fullscreen.
For anyone testing or redrawing the game: every card can carry a note of how it felt, and the page has an asset sheet of every background and sprite.

Each chapter now says why it reads the way it does, as one small spell at the top: “Read this way because…”. Every line says where it came from (your own setting, a link you followed, your carries, the book’s own). Change a line and read the chapter again, or copy a link that reads it your way for whoever opens it.
Chapter Fifteen is now Pupil, Parcel, or Door: the night school the stranger turns up at is where grown-ups learn their letters after the day’s work, and he is written on its roll as a pupil.
At BoonWAP’s table in Chapter Six, the porter showing a glassed folio is showing it to his own children.

The map-house has a round map now, for things that will not lie flat: every thread, voice, wonder and material in the book, folded so that whatever you look at opens out. Ask it something in Spw (try #egg @boof, or $glass) and watch the question run through the chapters. It is on the Topics page.
At the end of each chapter, you can follow what it is made of: the glass, the flour, the frost, the oak. Each one leads to the next chapter where it comes back strongest.

Three new wonders in Book Two, if you look closely: frill-lichen on the old stone, remainder-moths round the lamps at the parcel gate, and the night school's sliver tin. Each gives something in Exactly One Pie.
Held chapters reach further: if Mimes Against WAP hold one, the entrance's pie drawer and the chapter's own pie doors say so, and ?[pie] at your desk lists every chapter's mark.

Carrying the pie through a chapter now leaves a mark on it: the chapter reads a little more like fairy tale, absurd reality or low magic depending on how the carry went. A note at the top of the chapter says so, with a switch to read it plainly.
If Mimes Against WAP out-do the pie in a chapter, they hold it, and it is harder to wonder about pie there: its pie words go quiet until you carry it through again and win it back.

The game introduces things as the book does, says what each one does the first time you meet it, and takes a breath at every section break. Beside the screen, a running tally shows how the chapter will be kept.

Exactly One Pie is now a voyage through the whole book: the screen holds still while each chapter goes by, its own words flowing past on one side and its wonders waiting on the other. Step ahead up the lanes to keep them; each gives the carry something.

Obstacles knock the pie instead of ending the carry: a red ring says which ones, and each knock shows how much it tilted (and what it took). The pie spills when the tilt is full. Flour no longer slows you, and a thin pie still satisfies a clown.

New in the lanes: hop over holes, ditches and anything low; clowns with appetites (pips over their heads) that bigger pies satisfy faster; slow beavers that slow the land and not you; and mimes, including Mimes Against WAP, who shake flour into the air for Mr. BaneWAP and gather him baneberries, which he is made of. Step on them first.

The entrance has a new door between the stones: carry the pie from the beginning, into Book Two, from where you stopped reading, or to the long table where the next stone is set. Your furthest carry is kept there too.

Mr. BoonWAP and Mr. BaneWAP say a little more in Chapters Six, Eleven, Twelve and Fifteen: BoonWAP talks past the room and says one true thing; BaneWAP announces his schemes, and, foiled, says one thing more than he means to. What they let slip in Exactly One Pie now points back to where you can read it.

In Exactly One Pie, Mr. BoonWAP and Mr. BaneWAP now let slip the land's lore: one true thing when BoonWAP holds court, one blurted secret when BaneWAP is foiled. More opens as you find more of the land — chapters, wonders, sightings, tellings — and the game page keeps every line.
What the pies say appears under the game now, like subtitles, never across it.
Throws are aimed: a needle sweeps from the pie. Posts bend a slice, walls bounce it, wasps and pigeons snatch it.
The pie is kept whole by an aura of flour and boonberries. Every slice draws on both, and a wasted slice costs more. Mr. BoonWAP tops it up.
Flour comes in bags and piles. A pile is a ramp for a thrown slice; throw at a bag and it bursts into one.
The game page shows what everything is, drawn by the game itself.

Exactly One Pie: Mr. BoonWAP, a sentient pie, holds court at the head of the lanes — clowns flock and every pie finds an eye — and Mr. BaneWAP meddles with announced schemes. He always leaves an off switch.
You can throw now: a slice up your lane. When the ring on a clown turns gold, a throw counts twice and steadies the pie.
Flour no longer spills the pie. It slows you down and pushes you back in the story.
The city comes in rows, and every row leaves a way through. Things are larger, quieter cobbles let them read first, and the lane you are in is lit.
Chapters Six, Eleven and Fifteen have doors into the game where its places happen, and the game sends you back to the very page you came from.

Exactly One Pie no longer stops at each new place: the change is said in a small note at the top of the game while the colours cross over and the carry goes on. When the hat moves on, the next carrier fades in under it.

The folio wall has a new shelf: folios from the maker's own worktable at spwashi.com — real pages, collaged, laminated and painted — each with the question it asks and where in the land it stands. Two of them hang beside Exactly One Pie.
Exactly One Pie: it is not always him under the hat. Each carry the hat settles on someone — the porter, a feast clerk, the Genie, now and then a clown — and at a change of scene it may move on.
Clowns love WAP: a pie in the face. Step into one and it gets the pie, square, with a WAP you can hear; the pie on the plate is no smaller. A toggle under the game turns the sound off.

Exactly One Pie, a small game: someone is destined to spill exactly one pie, and a figure in a hat is carrying one up the lanes of Bonk City. Step across the city as it streams at you; hurry and the pie tilts; Boof steadies it if you pass her. Find it under the hat on the home page, or at the desk with @[pie].

A chapter opened from such a link says so under its title, with Keep as mine and Let go. Nothing a link sets becomes yours unless you keep it.

At the desk, ?[links] lists everything a link can carry.

The home page's look has moved out of the top bar and into the story: at the folio house by the parcel gate, the binder keeps six covers on pegs. Tap the underlined words in her sentence to change the cover, the lamp and the shutters.
One book, one binding: the cover you choose at the folio house binds every chapter, and a cover chosen in a chapter's Reading nook binds the home page.
Phrases with a faint wavy line are told more than one way. Tap one to hear its next telling; hold it to see every telling as a card, the ones you have not heard yet face down.
Other tellings, in the rail: turn the hour and every phrase rolls to that hour's words while the light walks with it. Back to now, or the book's own words, whenever you like.
Bind the book: Reading nook → Binding has six spines — rag paper, Bonk glass, salt flat, hearth clay, slate & chalk, starfield.
Begin again, beside Continue reading or under the contents: from the top, keeping everything, or a fresh copy whose marks are set aside so you can put them back.
On a wide screen the page and its rail sit together in the middle, with the room around them.

Frame this and the light table have Copy stage link: the light, the words and the frame you tuned, as a link anyone can open.
The light table has named cues — dawn, morning, noon, afternoon, dusk, night, lamp — beside the sky you can drag.
The trial once called a living page is now plainly named: Phrases turn with the clock.
A light you hold now stays where you put it while you scroll.

Hold the light: at the end of every section, open the light table and drag the sun across a small sky, turn the scene's warmth, glow, ink, grain and edge, or carry the light with you until you set it down. Each scene's motif already leans its light a little: an egg holds amber low, a hat is pencil on paper, a torch keeps the dark close. Tap a wonder and the light leans toward it.

Frame this: set the passage you are reading on a card — story, square or card proportions — with the chapter's name and address, the type size and the light at hand. The controls step back so the screenshot is clean.

At the table: every chapter now ends with a closed page for playing in it — the place, its light, its people and what they want, three hooks, a d6, things worth carrying out, a bracework move, and the page's own dice.

Sayings: the land's makers have rules they live by — first ink stays; glass over, never scrape; chalk is cheaper than oak — and they travel from chapter to chapter. Tap one to keep it; each has a second reading, in the workshop.

A living page, to try (Switches → A living page, or any chapter with ?try=living): a few phrases in every chapter breathe, turning by the minute, the hour or the day — away from wherever you are reading. The marks glint now and then, like grains in soil. Switch it off and every word is the book's own again.

Bracework in the chapters: where the land's makers write in sigils and braces — the council's law, a brace-box, the joiners' marks, the archive's catalogue, the clerk's new form — the page now reads it with the Spw interpreter and draws what it found.
Every chapter ends by naming the wonders it holds; each is a door to its page in your almanac.
Kept wonders in the almanac now offer a plate prompt: the scene in words, ready to paint from.

Every chapter was revised for the land itself: more of what things are made of, what they smell like, who keeps them, and what lives in the wild places — echo-wrens and salt-whales, pane-snails and seam-otters, kilns and needles and bells.

The first time a chapter names a creature, a contrivance or a piece of bracework, it is marked with a dotted line. Tap it to keep it in your almanac; the card says where else it lives, so finding it again somewhere new fills in its entry.

A new page, the Almanac, keeps what you have found — with silhouettes of what is still out there, the drawing of the figure under the hat, and a combining bench where found things become small realms in braces. (Switches → Wonders in the prose turns the marks off.)
At the desk, ?[almanac] counts what you have kept.

Keep an eye out for the figure under the hat. Each time you notice him, in the margins or the story, a small card says so and his drawing gains a line. Nine sightings, nine strokes. (Switches → Sightings turns the cards off; they are still kept.)

The home page answers back: drawers remember what you have found and stamp it, the land riffles before it chooses, the egg turns when you change its reading, new chapters turn to read once you have read them, and the next stone counts down.

The egg can be seen three ways on the home page — opal, stone, amber — and the material cabinet keeps what you have noticed.

X-ray reading, in Switches: hover a word, a sentence or a paragraph and the structure shows through — the threads a word belongs to, the way a sentence leans, the sign a paragraph sits under. Click to hold it.

A folio wall: pages under glass, the maker's first. New folios stay liquid until a stone day passes, then go clear.
The ants under the berry rows have torches now, and streets; the Genie, it turns out, did good business with them.
Boof works for the land, not for fruit — a slip that had lingered in the copy is mended everywhere it stood.
